Not an Obama fan on the whole (voted for Trump, or rather against Hillary) but some of what Obama did wasn't inherently bad just because Obama did it. Case in point Title II protections for the Internet.

It's not quite fair to say "it wasn't broken before" when you ponder whether Obama's Title II protections were necessary. The Internet was (and still is) growing. Back in the post-ARPA Golden Age it was a given that all types of IP traffic (protocol packets) would be treated equally. Why wouldn't they, after all? A data network is a data network. The only thing that mattered was bandwith -- how fast you could pass packets. A consumer would pay for a connection as fast as needed to access remote services. Remote services would pay for connections as fast as needed to serve the combined speed demands of all of their consumers. And in the middle was this magic backbone transport. All of the telecom players that wanted to get in the longhaul business got their money by providing the most reliable and fastest backbone transports possible.

When the Internet became commonplace the stage was set for a big problem. In many places the only option for last-mile users to connect to this Internet with decent transport speeds was via broadband-over-cable (DOCSIS) using the infrastructure cable television providers had in place. To begin with cable companies just made a buck providing high-speed access to this agnostic network that was the Internet. Mundane data things like e-mail or transferring a file didn't matter to them. Neither did VoIP much, though some providers chose to make an extra buck selling phone services now. Then streaming services like Netflix emerged. Just packets passing data. But this data cut right into the heart of the cable companies' wallet. So companies changed strategies a little. Cable companies (and wireless providers like Verizon) started looking for extra ways to cash in, like setting up their own streaming services to compete with Netflix, Pandora, Spotify, Hulu, etc... And here the big ugly problem emerged -- the same company trying to sell a service (Comcast Xfinity streaming, for example) is also in charge of managing the network that can connect you to competing alternatives, and degrade those alternatives unless "protection money" was exacted from the respective competing companies or the user paid a surcharge just to have a choice.

Title II was created back in the days when the old "one national phone company" of Ma Bell was forced to break up. Turns out Bell Telephone would make it work nice if two Bell customers dialed each other but, if one party was in a region that Bell had been forced to turn over to competing phone companies, then those calls were degraded and problematic. This was ruled as illegal and unfair competitive practices. Obama and others saw that the Internet was on the cusp of having the same problems emerge and so Title II protections were extended to ISPs as well.

The problem distills down to data connection providers who are also allowed to be data content providers being allowed to control the connection to favor their services over alternatives.

The other emerging problem is slightly harder to put into analogy but you will see it soon. The Internet is a communications conduit. Imagine the old phone company being allowed to charge extra just so you could call all of your family, or maybe have no restrictions on which businesses in town you could call. Something like "Your basic phone plan doesn't let you call Blockbuster Video because we have a movie rental business in town." That kind of thing. That's about to happen.

Kiss your window into the wide open world goodbye once enforced neutrality is gone. It's not about Big Government restricting capitalism and the free market, it's about acknowledging that there needs to be an open, common-carrier conduit and that provision of that conduit is a business in itself -- conduit providers must not be allowed to block or extort traffic on the conduit.

One of the few (IMO) good thing Obama did was head off a problem. It's not that "it wasn't broken before," more that "it was about to be broken and was averted."
